identity.title: Muscle pain/weakness, prolonged immobilization or exertion, dark cola-colored urine

technique.how: Ask about muscle pain, weakness, swelling and dark tea/cola-coloured urine, and exposures: found down/prolonged immobilization, seizure, extreme exertion or heat, crush or trauma, cocaine/amphetamines, alcohol, statins/fibrates, antipsychotics (NMS), recent infection. Palpate for tender, swollen or tense muscle compartments and check distal pulses and sensation.
technique.prerequisites: Collateral history for obtunded or intoxicated patients; medication and drug-use review.

interpretation.positive_finding: Myalgia or weakness with dark urine after immobilization, exertion, seizure or toxin exposure strongly suggests rhabdomyolysis; check CK and a urine dipstick (heme-positive without red cells).
interpretation.negative_finding: Absent muscle symptoms or dark urine do not exclude rhabdomyolysis; many cases are oligosymptomatic and even qualitative urine myoglobin was positive in only 19% of 475 inpatients (PMID 16267412, Abstract). Measure CK whenever risk factors exist.
interpretation.pitfalls: Dark urine also comes from hematuria, hemoglobinuria or bilirubin. In 60% of cases multiple causes co-exist and toxins account for 46% (PMID 16267412, Abstract); CK peaks at 24–72 h, so an early value may be modest (unverified recall).
interpretation.changes_what: Positive → CK, creatinine, potassium, urinalysis; start IV fluids; assess compartments. Negative → still send CK if found down, post-seizure or toxin-exposed.

sources.citation: Bosch X, Poch E, Grau JM. Rhabdomyolysis and acute kidney injury. The New England journal of medicine 2009. Narrative review (N Engl J Med 2009;361:62-72).
Melli G, Chaudhry V, Cornblath DR. Rhabdomyolysis: an evaluation of 475 hospitalized patients. Medicine 2005.
Gabow PA, Kaehny WD, Kelleher SP. The spectrum of rhabdomyolysis. Medicine 1982. Medicine (Baltimore) 1982;61(3):141-52; no abstract on PubMed.

safety_scope.do_not_use_when: Do not exclude rhabdomyolysis by history in obtunded, intoxicated or found-down patients — send CK.
safety_scope.escalation_warning: Tense painful compartment, hyperkalemia or rising creatinine → urgent surgical and nephrology involvement.
safety_scope.interobserver_note: History items; no reliability data found.

extraction_notes: Anchor PMID 19571284 confirmed (Bosch et al. NEJM 2009 review; PubMed has no abstract). No diagnostic-accuracy study of the history items against CK-defined rhabdomyolysis was found ('rhabdomyolysis hospitalized patients clinical presentation myalgia weakness urine'; 'rhabdomyolysis 475 hospitalized patients'; 'The spectrum of rhabdomyolysis[Title]'; 'Gabow rhabdomyolysis spectrum 1982 Medicine Baltimore'). Melli 2005 (PMID 16267412; 475 inpatients with CK >5× ULN) abstract gives etiology and urine-myoglobin figures but no myalgia/dark-urine frequencies; Gabow 1982 (PMID 7078398) confirmed but PubMed carries no abstract, so its classic symptom frequencies could not be quoted. Status not_quantified; numbers in pitfalls/negative_finding are quoted from the Melli abstract: 'Urine myoglobin detected by dipstick/ultrafiltration was positive in only 19%'; 'In 60% of all cases, multiple factors were present'; 'illicit drugs, alcohol, and prescribed drugs responsible for 46%' (all Abstract, Results).
